title: Overfitting, bias and variance, regularization
html:
Purpose. The most common way a model fails is not that it learned too little, but that it learned the wrong thing: the noise in its training data. Understanding this failure, and the tools against it, is what separates a working model from a demo that falls apart on real data.

Key ideas

  • Underfitting (high bias): too simple, bad on training data and on new data.
  • Overfitting (high variance): too flexible, great on training data, bad on new data.
  • The test error is U-shaped as flexibility grows, while the training error only goes down. The gap between them is the warning sign.
  • Regularization adds a penalty on large weights to the cost. It trades a little training accuracy for better behaviour on new data. The strength is lambda.

11.1 Underfit, about right, overfit

The same fourteen noisy points, fitted three ways. The straight line is too simple: it misses the curve in the data (underfitting). The gentle curve follows the real pattern. The wiggly curve passes close to every dot, but between the dots it swings wildly, and it will predict badly for a new input (overfitting). Ng's housing version: a straight line does not follow the price curve, a quadratic is a reasonable fit, and a high-order polynomial hits every training house exactly and gives absurd prices in between.

The goal is generalization: doing well on data the model has not seen. A model that memorizes its training set is like a student who learned last year's exam answers by heart.

The same happens in classification. An overfit decision boundary twists around individual points; a good one is smooth.

11.2 Bias and variance

StatQuest's Bias and Variance video (7 minutes) gives the standard words for the two failures:

  • Bias is the systematic miss of a model that is too simple to follow the true pattern. A straight line through a curve is wrong in the same way on every dataset.
  • Variance is how much a model changes when you give it a different sample of data. A very flexible model fits whatever noise it was shown, so a different sample gives a very different curve.

The figure averages 200 runs on data from a wavy curve plus noise. The test error is the error on new data. For a straight line (degree 1) it is 0.293, for a cubic (degree 3) it is 0.120, and for a degree 11 polynomial it is 0.372. At the same time the training error keeps falling, to 0.013 at degree 11. A model that scores nearly perfectly on its own training data can be the worst on new data. This is the bias-variance trade-off: simpler models have more bias and less variance, flexible ones the reverse, and the best model sits in between. Infinite Codes calls it the single most important idea in machine learning.

11.3 Diagnosing which problem you have

Compare the error on the training set with the error on a validation set (Chapter 3). The numbers tell you which way you are wrong:

Training error Validation error Diagnosis What to try
High High, similar High bias (underfitting) More features, a more flexible model, less regularization
Low Much higher High variance (overfitting) More data, fewer features, a simpler model, more regularization
Low Low, similar Good Stop

(Ng covers this properly in course 2, "advice for applying machine learning". For now, the habit is enough: always look at both numbers.)

11.4 Three remedies for overfitting

  1. Collect more data. With many more examples the wiggly curve cannot pass through all of them. It is the best cure but often impossible.
  2. Use fewer features (or lower the polynomial degree). Pick the most relevant ones; this is called feature selection. A downside: you throw away information.
  3. Regularize. Keep all the features but stop any single weight from becoming huge (Ng, video 38).

11.5 Regularization

The wiggles of an overfit model come from large weights: the model needs big numbers to bend sharply. So add a penalty for large weights to the cost, and training has to balance fit against simplicity:

J(w⃗,b)=12m∑i=1m(fw⃗,b(x⃗(i))−y(i))2+λ2m∑j=1nwj2J(\vec{w},b) = \frac{1}{2m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( f_{\vec{w},b}(\vec{x}^{(i)}) - y^{(i)} \right)^2 + \frac{\lambda}{2m} \sum_{j=1}^{n} w_j^2
  • The first term is the usual error: fit the data. The second is the new penalty: keep the weights small.
  • lambda (a hyperparameter you choose) sets the balance. With lambda = 0 there is no penalty, and you are back to the original model. With a huge lambda the weights are pushed to almost zero and the model becomes nearly flat, which underfits.
  • The bias b is usually not penalized (Ng, video 39).
  • Dividing by 2m, as in the first term, keeps lambda comparable across datasets of different size.

In gradient descent the only change is one extra term in the update of each weight (Ng, videos 40 and 41, for linear and logistic regression):

wj:=wj−α[1m∑i=1m(fw⃗,b(x⃗(i))−y(i))xj(i)+λmwj]w_j := w_j - \alpha \left[ \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( f_{\vec{w},b}(\vec{x}^{(i)}) - y^{(i)} \right) x_j^{(i)} + \frac{\lambda}{m} w_j \right]

Rearranged, it reads w_j (1 - alpha lambda / m) minus the usual step. On every iteration the weight is first shrunk by a tiny factor, and then moved as before. That is why this penalty is also called weight decay. For logistic regression the formula is identical; only f is the sigmoid.

11.6 L2 and L1

Beyond the videos. The penalty above, the sum of squared weights, is called L2 regularization, or ridge. The alternative is L1 (lasso), which adds the sum of the absolute values of the weights. L1 tends to push some weights exactly to zero, so it also selects features. Elastic net mixes the two. StatQuest has short videos on each, and "Ridge vs Lasso, Visualized" shows why L1 gives zeros.

11.7 Regularization in practice

In scikit-learn, lambda is called alpha in Ridge, and for LogisticRegression the setting is C, where C = 1 / lambda (small C means strong regularization). I checked both against a handmade gradient descent with the formulas above, and they match exactly.

The experiment below fits a degree 10 polynomial to 15 noisy points with different regularization strengths, and averages over 200 random datasets:

import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
truth = lambda x: np.sin(2 * np.pi * x * 0.8)                   # the pattern we pretend not to know
x_test = rng.uniform(0, 1, 2000)
y_test = truth(x_test) + rng.normal(0, 0.25, 2000)

alphas = [1e-6, 1e-2, 1, 100]                                    # alpha is scikit-learn's name for lambda
train_err = np.zeros(len(alphas)); test_err = np.zeros(len(alphas))
runs = 200
for _ in range(runs):                                            # average over 200 small random datasets
    x = np.linspace(0, 1, 15)
    y = truth(x) + rng.normal(0, 0.25, 15)
    for i, a in enumerate(alphas):
        model = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(10), StandardScaler(), Ridge(alpha=a))
        model.fit(x[:, None], y)
        train_err[i] += np.mean((model.predict(x[:, None]) - y) ** 2) / runs
        test_err[i] += np.mean((model.predict(x_test[:, None]) - y_test) ** 2) / runs

for a, tr, te in zip(alphas, train_err, test_err):
    print(f"alpha {a:<8} train error {tr:.3f}   test error {te:.3f}")
Alpha (lambda) Train error Test error Reading
0.000001 0.029 0.092 almost no penalty: fits the training data best, worse on new data
0.01 0.041 0.082 a little penalty: training error rises, test error falls
1 0.117 0.128 too much: starting to underfit
100 0.292 0.302 far too much: nearly flat, both errors high

The lesson is in the shape: as lambda grows, the training error only rises, while the test error falls first and then rises. The noise in this data limits the best possible test error to about 0.06, so the gain from 0.092 to 0.082 is a real share of what was available. You choose lambda the same way you choose any hyperparameter: try several values and keep the one with the best validation error (Chapter 12), never the best training error.

Loan example. Suppose you have 3,000 labelled applications and 60 candidate features, many of them overlapping (amount, amount per term, monthly cost, income, debt ratio). With so few rows and so many columns, an unregularized model will find accidental patterns. Regularization, plus a validation set to pick lambda, is the standard defence. A simple, strongly regularized logistic regression is a very hard baseline to beat on a table like this.

Common mistakes

  • Judging a model by training error alone.
  • Choosing lambda by the test set (then the test set is no longer a fair judge).
  • Forgetting to scale features before regularizing: the penalty treats all weights alike, so unscaled features are penalized unfairly.
  • Making the model more flexible whenever it is wrong, without checking whether the error is bias or variance.

Check yourself

  • Your training error is 2% and your validation error is 18%. What is the problem and what are two remedies?
  • What happens to the weights as lambda becomes very large?
  • Why is a model that is perfect on its training data suspicious?
  • In scikit-learn, which C corresponds to a lambda of 10?
Show answers

(1) High variance (overfitting). Remedies: more data, fewer features, a simpler model, more regularization. (2) They shrink towards zero and the model becomes almost flat (underfitting). (3) It may have memorized the noise, so it will probably do worse on new data. (4) C = 1 / 10 = 0.1.
